# Configure Auth0 for agent IAM

@include 'alerts/enterprise-and-hcp.mdx'

Configure users, OIDC applications, and Actions in Auth0 to issue tokens with
Rich Authorization Request (RAR) claims for Vault Enterprise agentic IAM.


## Before you start

- **You must have an Auth0 tenant with
  an [Auth0 Enterprise](https://auth0.com/pricing) license**. Vault agentic IAM
  uses Auth0
  [Custom Token Exchange](https://auth0.com/docs/authenticate/custom-token-exchange)
  to add RAR claims to access tokens, and Custom Token Exchange requires a paid
  Enterprise license.

- **You must have sufficient permission for your Auth0 tenant**. You must have
  permission to create resources (applications, APIs, users, and Actions) and
  to use the Auth0 Management API.

- **You must have the [`oauth2c`](https://github.com/SecureAuthCorp/oauth2c) CLI**
  installed and in your system `PATH` to interact with OAuth 2.0 authorization
  servers.

- **You must have `curl` and [`jq`](https://jqlang.org/)** installed to call the
  Auth0 Management API and the Auth0 token endpoint.

<Highlight title="Try the tutorial">

To walk through a robust, end-to-end agentic IAM workflow using Docker
containers, we also offer an in-depth tutorial on
[Securing agent permissions with Vault](/vault/tutorials/enterprise/secure-agent-permissions-with-vault).

</Highlight>


## Step 1: Create a custom API

1. Navigate to **Applications** > **APIs**.

1. Click **Create API**.

1. In the **Name** field, enter a name value (for example, `vault-api`).

1. In the **Identifier** field, provide the API address of your Vault cluster.
   The identifier value eventually becomes the JWT `aud` claim.

1. For **JSON Web Token (JWT) Profile**, select **RFC 9068**.

1. Scroll down and click **Create**.

1. Click the **Settings** tab.

1. Scroll down to **RBAC Settings**.

1. Click the toggle to switch on **Enable RBAC**.

1. Click the toggle to switch on **Add Permissions in the Access Token**.

1. Click **Save**.


## Step 2: Create an Auth0 application

1. Navigate to **Applications** > **Applications**, then click
   **Create Application**.

1. Enter a custom name for the **Name** field.

1. Select **Regular Web Application** for the application type.

1. Click **Create**.

1. Open the **Settings** page and note the **Client ID**, **Domain**, and
   **Client Secret** for your application.

1. Scroll to **Application URIs** section.

1. Add the default callback for `oauth2c` to the **Allowed Callback URLs** list,
   `http://localhost:9876/callback`, so `oauth2c` can receive the authorization
   code when you sign in.

1. Click **Advanced Settings**.

1. Click **OAuth**.

1. In the **Allowed APPs/APIs** field, enter your Vault API address (for example,
   `https://<vault-addr>:8200/v1`).

1. Open the **Grant Types** tab and check **Authorization Code**.

1. Open the **Endpoints** tab and record both the **OAuth Authorization URL**
   and the **JSON Web Key Set URL** values for use later.

1. Click **Save**.


## Step 3: Grant application access

With the API and application both created, you need to grant client access from
the API to the application.

1. Navigate to **Auth0 Dashboard** > **Applications** > **APIs**.

1. Select the API you created.

1. Click **Application Access**.

1. Find your application, and click **Edit**.

1. Click **Grant Access**.

1. Click the **Always grant all permissions** checkbox.

1. Click **Save**.


## Step 4: Create an agent user

1. Navigate to **User Management** > **Users**.

1. Click **Create User**.

1. Select **Create via UI** or **Create via JSON**.

1. Enter the appropriate information for **Email** and **Password**.

1. Click **Create**.

1. On the user page, click **Edit** next to **Email**, and mark the email as
   verified.


## Step 5: Obtain a Management API token

The [Auth0 Management API](https://auth0.com/docs/api/management/v2) lets you
manage your tenant programmatically. You need a Management API access token to
enable Custom Token Exchange and to create a token exchange profile.

1. Navigate to **Applications** > **APIs** and click **Auth0 Management API**.

1. Open the **Advanced** tab.

1. Click **Create and Authorize Test Application**. Auth0 creates an
   application that can connect to your tenant through the Management API.

1. Open the **API Explorer** tab and copy the token.

1. Save the application domain and the Management API token as environment
   variables:

    ```shell-session
    $ export                                        \
        APP_DOMAIN="<your_tenant>.<region>.auth0.com" \
        MGMT_TOKEN="<management_api_token>"
    ```

The Management API token expires after one day (86400 seconds). Repeat this step
to get a new token if you continue configuring your tenant after the token
expires.


## Step 6: Enable Custom Token Exchange for the application

1. Save the client ID of the application you created as an environment
   variable:

    ```shell-session
    $ export APP_ID="<application_client_id>"
    ```

1. Use the Management API to allow your application to use Custom Token
   Exchange profiles:

    ```shell-session
    $ curl --request PATCH                                   \
        --url "https://${APP_DOMAIN}/api/v2/clients/${APP_ID}" \
        --header "Authorization: Bearer ${MGMT_TOKEN}"         \
        --header "Content-Type: application/json"              \
        --data '{
          "token_exchange": {
            "allow_any_profile_of_type": ["custom_authentication"]
          }
        }'
    ```

1. Confirm that the response includes the `token_exchange` setting and that
   both `is_first_party` and `oidc_conformant` are `true`. Token exchange fails
   unless both values are `true`. For example:

    <CodeBlockConfig hideClipboard>

    ```json
    {
      "name": "HashiCups Vault",
      "is_first_party": true,
      "oidc_conformant": true,
      "token_exchange": {
        "allow_any_profile_of_type": [
          "custom_authentication"
        ]
      },
      "app_type": "regular_web",
      ...
    }
    ```

    </CodeBlockConfig>


## Step 7: Create a Custom Token Exchange Action

Auth0 [Actions](https://auth0.com/docs/customize/actions) extend Auth0 at key
points in the authentication lifecycle. The Custom Token Exchange Action
verifies the incoming access token, sets the user for the new token, and passes
the requested `authorization_details` to the post-login Action you create in
the next step.

1. Navigate to **Actions** > **Library**.

1. Click **Create Action** and choose **Create Custom Action**.

1. Enter `process_rar_token_cte` for **Name**.

1. Select **Custom Token Exchange** as the trigger.

1. Keep **Node 22** as the runtime and click **Create**.

1. Replace the Action code with the following code. Replace
   `<your_tenant>.<region>.auth0.com` with your application domain and
   `<application_client_id>` with your application client ID:

    ```javascript
    const { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify } = require('jose');

    // Initialize the JWKS set outside the handler to cache public keys
    // across warm executions
    const AUTH0_DOMAIN = '<your_tenant>.<region>.auth0.com';
    const EXPECTED_ISSUER = `https://${AUTH0_DOMAIN}/`;
    const JWKS_URL = new URL(`https://${AUTH0_DOMAIN}/.well-known/jwks.json`);
    const JWKS = createRemoteJWKSet(JWKS_URL);

    // Applications allowed to call the token exchange
    const ALLOWED_CLIENT_IDS = new Set([
      '<application_client_id>'
    ]);

    // Validate the signature, issuer, expiration, and RS256 algorithm
    async function verifyTenantJwt(token) {
      const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, JWKS, {
        issuer: EXPECTED_ISSUER,
        algorithms: ['RS256'],
        clockTolerance: '10s'
      });
      return payload;
    }

    exports.onExecuteCustomTokenExchange = async (event, api) => {
      // 1. Authorize the calling application
      if (!ALLOWED_CLIENT_IDS.has(event.client.client_id)) {
        return api.access.deny('invalid_client', 'Client is not authorized for token exchange.');
      }

      // 2. Verify the subject token
      const subjectToken = event.transaction?.subject_token;
      if (!subjectToken) {
        return api.access.rejectInvalidSubjectToken('Missing required subject_token.');
      }

      let subjectPayload;
      try {
        subjectPayload = await verifyTenantJwt(subjectToken);
      } catch (err) {
        return api.access.rejectInvalidSubjectToken(`Subject token verification failed: ${err.message}`);
      }

      if (!subjectPayload.sub) {
        return api.access.rejectInvalidSubjectToken('Subject token does not contain a "sub" claim.');
      }

      // Set the user for the issued token
      api.authentication.setUserById(subjectPayload.sub);

      // 3. Pass the RAR details to the post-login Action
      const rawRar = event.request.body?.authorization_details;
      if (rawRar) {
        let parsedRar = rawRar;
        if (typeof rawRar === 'string') {
          try {
            parsedRar = JSON.parse(rawRar);
          } catch {
            return api.access.deny('invalid_request', 'Invalid JSON in authorization_details.');
          }
        }
        api.user.setAppMetadata('transient_rar_details', parsedRar);
      }
    };
    ```

1. Click **Deploy**.

1. Copy the Action ID from the end of the Action URL in your browser. For
   example, the Action ID for
   `https://manage.auth0.com/dashboard/us/<tenant>/actions/library/details/90f84643-f983-43f5-93a8-56c19f7dd7f4`
   is `90f84643-f983-43f5-93a8-56c19f7dd7f4`.

1. Save the Action ID as an environment variable:

    ```shell-session
    $ export CTE_ACTION_ID="<action_id>"
    ```


## Step 8: Create a Custom Token Exchange profile

Auth0 runs a Custom Token Exchange Action when a token request uses the
`subject_token_type` linked to that Action in a
[token exchange profile](https://auth0.com/docs/authenticate/custom-token-exchange/configure-custom-token-exchange#create-custom-token-exchange-profile).

Use the Management API to link the
`urn:vault:params:oauth:token-type:access_token` token type to your Action:

```shell-session
$ curl --request POST                                       \
    --url "https://${APP_DOMAIN}/api/v2/token-exchange-profiles" \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer ${MGMT_TOKEN}"             \
    --header "Content-Type: application/json"                  \
    --data '{
      "name": "custom_profile",
      "subject_token_type": "urn:vault:params:oauth:token-type:access_token",
      "action_id": "'"${CTE_ACTION_ID}"'",
      "type": "custom_authentication"
    }'
```


## Step 9: Add RAR claims with a post-login Action

The post-login Action reads the `authorization_details` that the Custom Token
Exchange Action stored, and adds them to the access token as a custom claim.

1. Navigate to **Actions** > **Library**.

1. Click **Create Action** and choose **Create Custom Action**.

1. Enter `inject_rar_claims_post_login` for **Name**.

1. Select **Login / Post Login** as the trigger.

1. Keep **Node 22** as the runtime and click **Create**.

1. Replace the Action code with the following code:

    ```javascript
    exports.onExecutePostLogin = async (event, api) => {
      const rarDetails = event.user.app_metadata?.transient_rar_details;
      const rarClaimNamespace = 'https://vault.hashicups.com';

      if (rarDetails) {
        // Add the custom claim under an HTTP/HTTPS namespace
        const CLAIM_KEY = rarClaimNamespace + '/authorization_details';
        api.accessToken.setCustomClaim(CLAIM_KEY, rarDetails);

        // Remove the transient user metadata
        api.user.setAppMetadata('transient_rar_details', null);
      }
    };

    exports.onContinuePostLogin = async (event, api) => {
      // Safe to leave empty if no external redirect is performed
    };
    ```

1. Click **Deploy**.

1. Navigate to **Actions** > **Triggers** and choose **post-login**.

1. Drag the `inject_rar_claims_post_login` Action from the **Add Action** pane
   between the **Start** and **Complete** nodes.

1. Click **Apply**.

Auth0 adds the RAR details to the access token under the
`https://vault.hashicups.com/authorization_details` claim rather than
`authorization_details`. When you create the OAuth resource server profile in
Vault, set
[`authorization_details_claim`](/vault/api-docs/system/config-oauth-resource-server)
to the custom claim name.


## Step 10: Capture a baseline token

Export the Auth0 values you recorded, then run `oauth2c` to confirm the trust
and to capture the `iss` and `sub` claims you need for the Vault profile and
entity aliases.

1. Save the Auth0 configuration values as environment variables. Replace the
   placeholders with your actual values from the Auth0 application settings:

    ```shell-session
    $ export \
        APP_AUTH_URL="https://<your_tenant>.<region>.auth0.com/authorize" \
        SECRET_VALUE="<application_client_secret>"                        \
        JWKS_URI="https://<your_tenant>.<region>.auth0.com/.well-known/jwks.json"
    ```

1. Save the Vault server address as `AUDIENCE_ADDR` so you can easily request
   the correct audience in the access token:

    ```shell-session
    $ export AUDIENCE_ADDR=${VAULT_ADDR}/v1
    ```

1. Request an access token using the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with
   PKCE:

    ```shell-session
    $ oauth2c "${APP_AUTH_URL}"           \
        --pkce                            \
        --client-id "${APP_ID}"           \
        --client-secret "${SECRET_VALUE}" \
        --response-types code             \
        --response-mode query             \
        --grant-type authorization_code   \
        --audience "${AUDIENCE_ADDR}"     \
        --auth-method client_secret_basic \
        --no-browser
    ```

    <Note>

    You must request the audience (`--audience https://<vault_addr>:8200/v1`) to
    receive a signed JWT. Without it, Auth0 returns an opaque token that Vault
    cannot validate.

    </Note>

1. Copy the URL that `oauth2c` prints under **Go to the following URL** and open
   it in a new private or incognito browser window. Sign in with the email
   address and password you set for the agent user, then close the private
   window after authentication succeeds.

1. After a successful sign-in, the terminal prints a success message along with
   a JSON object with the decoded access token. For example:

    <CodeBlockConfig hideClipboard>

    ```json
    {
      "aud": "https://localhost:8200/v1",
      "client_id": "EBYeLHzuLqSeyUYLY7EC3hqRgvaiS9Dv",
      "exp": 1782402664,
      "iat": 1782316264,
      "iss": "https://hashicups-dev.us.auth0.com/",
      "jti": "baFC3mowpruhSr1JdDRhbJ",
      "permissions": [],
      "sub": "auth0|c0ff33a2dc1f8e9de0dd95d7"
    }
    ```

    </CodeBlockConfig>

1. Save the `iss` and `sub` values to environment variables. The `sub` value
   contains a pipe character, so make sure to wrap the string in quotes:

    ```shell-session
    $ export                                         \
        ISSUER="https://hashicups-dev.us.auth0.com/" \
        EXTERNAL_ID='auth0|c0ff33a2dc1f8e9de0dd95d7'
    ```

1. Save the encoded `access_token` value from the `oauth2c` response as an
   environment variable:

    ```shell-session
    $ export SUBJECT_TOKEN="<access_token>"
    ```


## Step 11: Request a token with RAR claims

Exchange the baseline token for a token that carries ephemeral permissions as
RAR claims. The `subject_token_type` must match the token type in your token
exchange profile.

1. Request the token from the Auth0 token endpoint:

    ```shell-session
    $ export AGENT_TOKEN=$(curl --silent --request POST                           \
        --url "https://${APP_DOMAIN}/oauth/token"                                 \
        --header "content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded"                \
        --data-urlencode "grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange" \
        --data-urlencode "client_id=${APP_ID}"                                    \
        --data-urlencode "client_secret=${SECRET_VALUE}"                          \
        --data-urlencode "audience=${AUDIENCE_ADDR}"                              \
        --data-urlencode "subject_token=${SUBJECT_TOKEN}"                         \
        --data-urlencode "subject_token_type=urn:vault:params:oauth:token-type:access_token" \
        --data-urlencode 'authorization_details=[{"type":"vault:path_access","path":"secret-v2/data/shared-secret/foo","capabilities":["create"]}]' \
        | jq -r '.access_token')
    ```

1. Decode `AGENT_TOKEN` with your preferred JWT tool and confirm the token
   includes the RAR details under the custom claim. For example:

    <CodeBlockConfig hideClipboard>

    ```json
    {
      "aud": "http://127.0.0.1:8200/v1",
      "client_id": "V6WXP35RRHFXilt8wrAiB4wgLgyuhIyY",
      "exp": 1787331677,
      "https://vault.hashicups.com/authorization_details": [
        {
          "capabilities": [
            "create"
          ],
          "path": "secret-v2/data/shared-secret/foo",
          "type": "vault:path_access"
        }
      ],
      "iat": 1787245277,
      "iss": "https://dev-h3k61byz2u2pze7d.us.auth0.com/",
      "jti": "3s5dRVumBBQzeoEnvbfmLN",
      "permissions": [],
      "sub": "auth0|6a86ee5c8ab798838f14110c"
    }
    ```

    </CodeBlockConfig>

If the token exchange fails, check **Monitoring** > **Logs** in the Auth0
dashboard for tenant events, and the **Action Logs** for `console.log` output
from your Actions.


## Step 12: Save your provider information

Confirm your subject and actor details from Auth0. To configure agentic IAM,
you must have the following information:

Value               | Environment variable | Description
------------------- | ---------------------- | -----------
Authorization URL   | `APP_AUTH_URL`         | Authorization URL of the application
Domain address      | `APP_DOMAIN`           | Domain of the application you registered in Auth0
Auth0 client ID     | `APP_ID`               | Client ID of the application you registered in Auth0
Issuer URL          | `ISSUER`               | `iss` URL for your application
JWT subject ID      | `EXTERNAL_ID`          | JWT claim for the agent user from your application (`sub`)
Key endpoint        | `JWKS_URI`             | URL where clients can download public keys (JWKS) from your application
Client secret value | `SECRET_VALUE`         | Client secret associated with your application
Audience address    | `AUDIENCE_ADDR`        | Vault cluster address including the API version, `/v1`
RAR claim name      | none                   | Custom claim that holds the RAR details (`https://vault.hashicups.com/authorization_details`)

If you have not already, we recommend setting the following environment variables
to make Vault configuration more convenient:

```shell-session
$ export                                \
   VAULT_ADDR="<your_vault_server_url>" \
   APP_AUTH_URL="<app_auth_url>"        \
   APP_DOMAIN="<app_domain>"            \
   APP_ID="<app_client_id>"             \
   ISSUER="<app_iss_url>"               \
   EXTERNAL_ID="<app_jwt_sub>"          \
   JWKS_URI="<app_jwks_url>"            \
   SECRET_VALUE="<app_client_secret>"   \
   AUDIENCE_ADDR="<aud_address>"
```

For example:

<CodeBlockConfig hideClipboard>

```shell-session
$ export                                                              \
   VAULT_ADDR="https://127.0.0.1:8200"                                \
   APP_AUTH_URL="https://abc-123if67e.us.auth0.com/authorize"         \
   APP_DOMAIN="abc-123if67e.us.auth0.com"                             \
   APP_ID="ABCD...abc"                                                \
   ISSUER="https://abc-123if67e.us.auth0.com/"                        \
   EXTERNAL_ID="auth0|c0ff33a2dc1f8e9de0dd95d7"                       \
   JWKS_URI="https://abc-123if67e.us.auth0.com/.well-known/jwks.json" \
   SECRET_VALUE="000000...000000"                                     \
   AUDIENCE_ADDR="https://127.0.0.1:8200/v1"
```

</CodeBlockConfig>
